events_chronological: On a hot day one summer, thirteen-year-old Junia Thorne finishes a play to be performed for her brother's homecoming.
Junia watches from an upstairs window as her sister Rosalind strips to her underwear and climbs into the fountain in front of Tom Vasey, the housekeeper's son.
Tom drafts a letter of apology to Rosalind, sends the obscene version by mistake, and Junia reads it on the way.
Junia walks in on Tom and Rosalind making love in the library and takes it for an assault.
The twins run off, and during the search Junia sees their cousin Cissy being raped in the dark and names Tom as the man.
Tom is arrested and taken away in front of the family, and Rosalind breaks with all of them.
Five years later Tom is released from prison into the army and is separated from his unit in the retreat across the continent.
Rosalind, now a nurse in the city, writes to Tom, and the two spend a few hours together on his leave.
Tom walks to the evacuation beach with two corporals and reaches a shore of burning vehicles, shot horses and thousands of waiting men.
Tom lies down in a cinema on the seafront and dies of septicaemia the night before the ships come.
Junia, eighteen, takes a nursing place in the city instead of the university place she was offered, and treats men brought back from the continent.
Junia learns that Cissy is marrying Neville Frome, the man who actually raped her.
Junia goes to Rosalind's flat, finds Tom there, and promises to recant her statement and set the truth down in writing.
Rosalind is killed when a bomb bursts the water main above an underground station.
Decades later the elderly Junia, dying and giving her last interview, admits that she never went to the flat and that Tom and Rosalind never saw each other again.
Junia says she gave the two of them in her novel the life they were never allowed, and the film shows them together at a seaside cottage.
nonlinear_category_reason: Forward apart from two earlier insertions: the soldier's leave cut into his walk to the beach, and his death held back behind the sister's nursing years.
syuzhet_notes: The summer afternoon is told forward but partly doubled, with the fountain and the library replayed once as the child misreads them and once as they happened. Told-order bullet 9 is a flashback to the soldier's leave, cut into the walk to the beach. The largest displacement comes at bullets 13-16, where the closing interview establishes that bullet 12 never happened at all and that the lovers had already died apart, years before the scene the film has just shown.
fabula_notes: Most of the film is the novelist's book rather than the story world, and the ending cancels one scene outright; the chronology here follows what the interview establishes as true, which puts both deaths before the flat scene the film depicts. The seaside cottage is explicitly named as an invention.
